original_question: Does every holomorphic map F : P^k → P^k of degree at least two have a repelling periodic point? Do meromorphic maps have periodic orbits? -sibony@anh.matups.fr
target_in_paper: A Scratchpad-style open problem in the dynamics portion of The Several Complex Variables Problem List, attributed to N. Sibony: the existence of a repelling periodic point for a holomorphic self-map of complex projective space of algebraic degree at least 2, together with the parallel existence question for meromorphic self-maps of projective space.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core mathematical content of the targeted problem: it asks about self-maps of projective space, restricts the holomorphic case to degree at least two, distinguishes the stronger conclusion 'repelling periodic point' from the weaker conclusion 'periodic orbit', and keeps the separate meromorphic question rather than folding it into the holomorphic one.
missing_details: The ambient space should be identified as complex projective space P^k(C), not an arbitrary projective space over an unspecified field.
For the holomorphic case, 'degree' should be stated as algebraic degree d >= 2.
It should be explicit that F is a self-map F:P^k(C)->P^k(C).

The second clause should inherit the same ambient setting: it is most naturally read as asking about meromorphic self-maps of P^k(C), not meromorphic maps in general between arbitrary complex manifolds.
A 'periodic point' should be defined as a point p for which F^n(p)=p for some n>=1; a periodic orbit is the finite forward orbit of such a point.
For the meromorphic case, one should say that all iterates involved in F^n(p) are defined along the orbit.
A 'repelling periodic point' should be defined in higher dimension: if p has period n, then every eigenvalue of D(F^n)_p has modulus greater than 1.
If one wants the question fully stand-alone, one should specify whether the period need only be some n>=1 or the exact/minimal period; existence only needs some n>=1.

Because the source paper is a problem list with Scratchpad items, the draft should be sharpened from conversational wording into one precise projective-space existence question without broadening beyond that setting.
refined_question: Let F:P^k(C)->P^k(C) be a holomorphic endomorphism of algebraic degree d>=2. Must F admit a repelling periodic point; that is, does there exist p in P^k(C) and n>=1 such that F^n(p)=p and every eigenvalue of D(F^n)_p has modulus greater than 1? More generally, if F is a meromorphic self-map of P^k(C), must F admit at least one periodic orbit on which all iterates are defined?
justification: The arXiv item math/9509202 is not a conventional theorem-paper but a problem list, and its abstract explicitly says that it contains a 'Scratchpad' section for conversational or vaguely formulated questions. That matches the style of your draft and argues for keeping the target narrow rather than replacing it by a broader modern dynamics problem. The nearest mathematical context is the Fornaess-Sibony work on projective-space dynamics: they prove existence of infinitely many periodic orbits for holomorphic self-maps in dimension 2 and study when periodic points are repelling outside the critical orbit, which explains why the natural sharpening of your draft is exactly the existence of at least one repelling periodic point for holomorphic endomorphisms of P^k. For the meromorphic clause, the same projective-space context should be kept; later expository work in the same line makes explicit that meromorphic self-maps of projective space need not have periodic points at all, showing that the second clause is a genuinely separate existence question and should not be merged with the first. So the faithful refinement is to state both questions in the same ambient setting P^k(C), make 'degree' algebraic, and define 'repelling' via the eigenvalues of D(F^n)_p.
